## Can someone else get your numbers?

In 2010, an influential economics paper found that growth falls sharply when government debt passes 90% of GDP. Governments cited it.

In 2013 a student tried to **reproduce** it from the authors' spreadsheet, and found rows left out of an average. The striking result shrank to a modest one.

<div class="keyline">A result nobody can reproduce is, scientifically, just a claim.</div>

::: notes
Reinhart and Rogoff (2010), "Growth in a Time of Debt"; Herndon, Ash and Pollin (2013).
The error was found because someone could rerun it. Make that possible for your own work.
:::

## Why analyses don't reproduce

| What goes wrong | The habit that prevents it |
|:--|:--|
| Different package versions | a **locked environment** |
| A variable you made by hand, then deleted the code | **render from scratch** |
| You fixed a typo in the CSV, in Excel | **never edit raw data**; change it in code |
| `C:\Users\anna\Downloads\data.csv` | **relative paths**: `data/raw/data.csv` |
| A random sample differs every run | **set a seed** |
| The data was never committed | commit it, and let **the check** catch it |

<p class="more">More: <a href="../../lectures/week-1#why-reproducibility-matters">Week 1</a></p>

## Start with a question data can answer

| Vague | Answerable |
|:--|:--|
| "Look at Stockholm's weather." | Has Stockholm's mean annual temperature changed since the late 1990s? |
| "Analyse electricity prices." | How much more did southern Sweden pay than the north in 2023–25? |
| "Is AI a bubble?" | How do three signs of a bubble compare with 1929 and 2000? |

<p>A good question names <b>what</b> you measure, <b>where</b> and <b>when</b>, and what you'll <b>compare</b>.</p>

## Your repository

```
<username>-assignments/
├─ hw1/
│  ├─ report.qmd     ← your report: text and code, seven sections
│  ├─ report.md      ← the rendered report (made by Quarto)
│  └─ data/raw/      ← data exactly as you got it, with its source
├─ hw2/ … hw5/
├─ example/          ← a worked example of a report
├─ pyproject.toml + uv.lock   or   renv.lock   ← the locked environment
└─ .github/workflows/check.yml                ← the reproducibility check
```

<p class="small muted">Same structure every time: a reader knows where to look, and everything generated can be remade with one command.</p>

## Lockfiles: "works on my machine" → works on every machine

- Your code depends on packages, and packages change.
- A **lockfile** records the exact version of every package.
- Anyone can rebuild the same environment from it:

```bash
uv sync                      # Python
Rscript -e "renv::restore()" # R
```

- Add a package with `uv add pandas` or `renv::install("dplyr")` + `renv::snapshot()`. Never edit the lockfile by hand.

## Quarto: text and code in one file

````markdown
## Analysis

```{{python}}
yearly = temps.groupby("year")["temp"].mean()
yearly.loc[2011:].mean() - yearly.loc[:2010].mean()
```

The later period is warmer by 0.82 °C.
````

- `quarto render` runs the code and writes `report.md` with the results and figures.
- The numbers in your text come **from** the code, not copied by hand.

```{=html}

```

::: twocol
- **branch:** a separate line of work per assignment, `hw1` and `hw2` next to `main`.
- **commit:** save a snapshot, with a message saying why.
- **push:** send your commits to GitHub.
- **pull request:** your hand-in; the check runs and the review happens there.

<p class="more">More: <a href="../../guide#hand-in-an-assignment">How to hand in</a></p>

## The check

When you open or update a pull request, GitHub starts a clean computer, installs your locked environment and renders your report.

- **Green:** your analysis reproduces. Anyone can get your numbers.
- **Red:** something only works on your computer. The log says what.

<p class="more">More: <a href="../../guide#when-the-check-is-red">When the check is red</a></p>

# Statistics: the basics {.divider}

<p class="muted">From Probability I to statistics, in fifteen minutes.</p>

## Probability ↔ statistics

| Probability (MT3001) | Statistics (now) |
|:--|:--|
| You know the model: $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ | You have the data: $x_1, \dots, x_n$ |
| What will the data look like? | What was the model? And how sure are you? |

Data are **observations of random variables**. Your mean $\bar x$ is one value of the random variable $\bar X$: another sample would have given another value.

<p class="more">More: <a href="../../statistics">Statistics: the basics</a></p>

## Our example: has Lund got warmer?

<img src="../../img/statistics/data.svg" alt="Mean annual temperature in Lund, 1997–2025, with the mean of 1997–2010 and of 2011–2025">

The later period is **0.82 °C** warmer. Is that real, or could weather alone do it?

::: notes
Lund, not Stockholm: Stockholm is HW1, and we don't give away the answer.
:::

## Notation: what is $\bar X$?

::: notation
| Symbol | What it is | Lund, 1997–2010 |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $n$ | the number of years | $n = 14$ |
| $X_1, \dots, X_n$ | each year's mean temperature, as a **random variable**: what the weather *could* give | |
| $x_1, \dots, x_n$ | the values we **observed** | 8.58, 8.43, 9.14, … °C (1997, 1998, 1999, …) |
| $\bar X = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i X_i$ | the sample mean as a **random variable**: other years' weather would give another value | |
| $\bar x = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i$ | the **number** we computed: one value of $\bar X$ | $\bar x = 8.89$ °C |
| $\mu$ | the **true** mean of the period's climate. Unknown: what we want to know | ? |
| $\sigma$, $s$ | spread of single years: $\sigma$ the true value, $s$ our estimate from the data | $s = 0.62$ °C |
:::

<p class="small">$\bar x$ is our <b>estimate</b> of $\mu$. Statistics asks: how far from $\mu$ could $\bar x$ be?</p>

::: notes
Capital letters are random variables (before we look), small letters are the numbers we got.
:::

## Single years scatter a lot

<img src="../../img/statistics/spread.svg" alt="Each year's mean temperature as a dot, for both periods, with mean plus and minus one standard deviation">

<p class="small">One year varies by about $s = 0.62$ °C. The difference we found, 0.82 °C, is not much larger.</p>

## Means scatter much less

<img src="../../img/statistics/sampling.svg" style="max-height:250px" alt="Simulated: single years scatter widely, means of 14 years scatter much less">

<p class="small"><b>What was simulated:</b> grey, 100,000 single years drawn from $N(8.89,\ 0.62^2)$. Red, 100,000 times: draw 14 such years and take their mean $\bar x$. The means cluster far closer to $\mu$.</p>

$$\operatorname{SE} = \operatorname{sd}(\bar X) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n} \approx \frac{s}{\sqrt n} = \frac{0.62}{\sqrt{14}} = 0.17 \text{ °C}$$

<p class="small muted">The <b>standard error</b> (SE) is the standard deviation of $\bar X$: how far $\bar x$ typically lands from $\mu$. To halve it, you need four times the data.</p>

## Where 1.96 comes from

:::: cols
::: {}
1. CLT: $\bar X \approx N(\mu,\ \operatorname{SE}^2)$.
2. Standardise: $Z = \dfrac{\bar X - \mu}{\operatorname{SE}} \approx N(0, 1)$.
3. For $N(0,1)$: $P(-1.96 \le Z \le 1.96) = 0.95$. 1.96 leaves **2.5% in each tail**.
4. Rearrange for $\mu$: $P\big(\bar X - 1.96\,\operatorname{SE} \le \mu \le \bar X + 1.96\,\operatorname{SE}\big) = 0.95$.
:::
::: {}
<img src="../../img/statistics/normal-95.svg" alt="The standard normal curve with the middle 95% between −1.96 and 1.96 shaded, and 2.5% in each tail">

<p class="small muted">Other levels: 90% → 1.64, 99% → 2.58.</p>
:::
::::

::: notes
1.96 is the 97.5% quantile of the standard normal. With only 14 years the t-distribution
gives 2.16, a slightly wider interval; 1.96 is the large-sample value, and the bootstrap avoids the choice.
:::

## A confidence interval for Lund

Put in the numbers for 1997–2010:

$$\bar x \pm 1.96\,\operatorname{SE} = 8.89 \pm 1.96 \cdot 0.17 = [8.56,\ 9.22] \text{ °C}$$

<img src="../../img/statistics/intervals.svg" style="max-height:260px" alt="20 simulated 95% intervals; 19 contain the true mean, one misses">

<p class="small">The <b>interval</b> is random, $\mu$ is fixed. "95%" is a property of the method: of 20 new samples, about 19 intervals cover $\mu$ and 1 misses.</p>

## The difference, with its uncertainty

- **Estimate:** $\bar x_b - \bar x_a = 9.71 - 8.89 = 0.82$ °C (2011–2025 minus 1997–2010).
- **Its SE:** for independent means the variances add, $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_b - \bar X_a) = \frac{\sigma_b^2}{n_b} + \frac{\sigma_a^2}{n_a}$, so

$$\operatorname{SE}_{\text{diff}} = \sqrt{\frac{s_b^2}{n_b} + \frac{s_a^2}{n_a}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.62^2}{15} + \frac{0.62^2}{14}} = 0.23 \text{ °C}$$

- **Interval:** $0.82 \pm 1.96 \cdot 0.23 = [0.37,\ 1.27]$ °C.

The whole interval is above zero: consistent with warming of 0.4 to 1.3 °C, **not** with no warming.

## The same, by computer: the bootstrap

:::: cols
::: {}
**What is done**

1. Draw 14 years **from the 14 of 1997–2010, with replacement**: some years twice, some not at all.
2. Do the same for the 15 years of 2011–2025.
3. Compute the difference of the two means.
4. Repeat **10,000 times**.
5. The middle 95% of the 10,000 differences is the interval: **[0.40, 1.26]** °C.
:::
::: {}
::: resample
<div><span class="lab">data</span><span>1997</span><span>1998</span><span>1999</span><span>2000</span><span>…</span><span>2010</span></div>
<div><span class="lab">draw 1</span><span>1998</span><span class="dup">1998</span><span>2000</span><span>1997</span><span>…</span><span>2004</span></div>
<div><span class="lab">draw 2</span><span>2010</span><span>1999</span><span>2003</span><span class="dup">2003</span><span>…</span><span>1997</span></div>
:::
<img src="../../img/statistics/bootstrap.svg" style="max-height:200px" alt="Histogram of the difference in 10,000 resampled datasets, with the middle 95% marked">
:::
::::

<p class="small muted">Why it works: the resampled datasets vary about as much as new real data would. No formula needed, and it works for almost any statistic.</p>

## Could it be chance? A test, step by step

:::: cols
::: {}
1. **Hypothesis** $H_0$: $\mu_b = \mu_a$. No warming: the 0.82 °C is weather alone.
2. **Test statistic:** how many SEs is the difference from 0? $z = \dfrac{0.82 - 0}{0.23} = 3.6$.
3. **If $H_0$ is true**, $Z \approx N(0,1)$: beyond ±1.96 only 5% of the time.
4. **p-value:** $P(|Z| \ge 3.6) \approx 0.0003$. Without warming, a difference this large would turn up about 3 times in 10,000.
5. **Conclusion:** $p < 0.05$, so we reject $H_0$. Same as: 0 is outside the 95% interval.
:::
::: {}
<img src="../../img/statistics/z-test.svg" alt="Standard normal curve under H0, with ±1.96 dashed and the observed z = 3.6 far in the right tail">
:::
::::

## The same test, by computer: shuffling

:::: cols
::: {}
**What is done**

<p class="intro">If $H_0$ is true, it doesn't matter which period a year belongs to. So:</p>

1. Put all 29 years in one pile.
2. Deal them out **at random**: 14 to "1997–2010", 15 to "2011–2025".
3. Compute the difference of the two means.
4. Repeat **10,000 times**.
5. How often is the difference at least as large as 0.82 °C? About **1 in 1,000**: $p \approx 0.001$.
:::
::: {}
<img src="../../img/statistics/permutation.svg" alt="Differences when the years are shuffled between the periods at random; the observed difference is far in the tail">

<p class="small muted">No normal distribution needed. Both ways, $p$ is far below 0.05.</p>
:::
::::

::: notes
The normal approximation gives 0.0003, the shuffle 0.001: with 29 years they differ a little,
but both say the same thing.
:::

## What a p-value is not

- **Not** the probability that $H_0$ is true.
- **Not** the size or importance of the effect: report the estimate and its interval.
- $p > 0.05$ does **not** show there is no effect: maybe too little data.

## Correlation and trend

<img src="../../img/statistics/trend.svg" alt="Lund annual mean temperature with a fitted straight line">

<p>Slope <b>0.54 °C per decade</b> (95% interval 0.28 to 0.79), $r = 0.62$. Correlation is not causation: here the cause comes from physics, not from this data.</p>

## The many-tests trap

<img src="../../img/statistics/many-tests.svg" style="max-height:330px" alt="20 tests on pure random noise; one has p below 0.05">

<p>Twenty tests on pure noise: one comes out "significant". Test many things and something always will. Decide what to test <b>before</b> you look.</p>

## Writing it up

<div class="keyline big" style="font-size:1.1em">The years 2011–2025 were on average 0.82 °C warmer in Lund than 1997–2010 (95% confidence interval 0.37 to 1.27 °C).</div>

- The **estimate**, with **units**.
- Its **uncertainty**.
- What it does **not** show: why, or what happens next.
